title: The Scotch Game — A Master Class

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6
beats.say: Welcome to the Scotch — the opening that asks its question on move three and refuses to wait. We reach the familiar crossroads: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6, White attacking the e5-pawn, Black defending it. The Italian and the Ruy now circle for a slow build. The Scotch does the opposite — it strikes the centre at once.
beats.sayShort: e5 — the open-game start; the Scotch won't wait.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4
beats.say: 3.d4! This is the whole idea. Instead of bracing the break with c3 like the Italian, White throws the d-pawn at e5 immediately. Black almost always takes — leaving the pawn would just lose it — and the centre cracks wide open on move three. The Scotch trades the slow positional squeeze for fast, free piece play in an open position.
beats.sayShort: d4! — strike the centre at once.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4
beats.say: 3…exd4 4.Nxd4 — and there sits the Scotch knight, planted on d4 in the centre of the board, eyeing c6, f5, and b5 at once. This is the opening's signature: a beautifully centralised knight and open lines for every piece. Edward Lasker's rule rings true — a knight on a strong central square is worth a tempo of development. The cost is that the symmetry is gone and the game turns sharp.
beats.sayShort: Nxd4 — the centralised Scotch knight dominates.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bc5
beats.say: Black's most principled reply: 4…Bc5, the Classical Variation. The bishop develops with tempo, attacking the d4-knight and pointing menacingly toward f2. White cannot ignore it — the knight is the pride of the position and must be defended. The fight is now about who controls d4.
beats.sayShort: …Bc5 — the Classical, hitting the d4-knight.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bc5 Be3 Qf6
beats.say: 5.Be3 defends the knight and stares back at the c5-bishop. Black piles on with 5…Qf6, a second attacker on d4 that also eyes f2 and the dark squares. The whole opening now balances on the d4-square — two White defenders, two Black attackers. White's next move is the quiet glue that holds it all together.
beats.sayShort: Be3 Qf6 — both pile onto d4.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bc5 Be3 Qf6 c3
beats.say: 6.c3 — modest but vital. The pawn adds a third support to the d4-knight and quietly takes the d4 and b4 squares away from Black's pieces. Now the tension is stable, and White can finish development knowing the centralised knight is rock-solid. From here the plans diverge into rich, open middlegame play.
beats.sayShort: c3 — a third support; the d4-knight is solid.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bc5 Be3 Qf6 c3 Nge7 Bc4
beats.say: 6…Nge7 develops the king-knight toward g6 and keeps the pawn structure intact, and White brings out the Italian bishop with 7.Bc4 — straight at f7, the soft square every open-game attack returns to. The pieces are flowing out fast; this is the Scotch's promise paying off — open lines, active bishops, a dominant knight.
beats.sayShort: Nge7 Bc4 — develop fast, the bishop eyes f7.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bc5 Be3 Qf6 c3 Nge7 Bc4 O-O O-O d6
beats.say: Both kings reach safety — 7…O-O 8.O-O — and Black plays 8…d6 to free his light-squared bishop and shore up the c5-bishop's diagonal. The position is balanced and tense, every piece nearly developed. Now White begins the trades and the pawn expansion that define the Classical Scotch middlegame.
beats.sayShort: O-O d6 — kings safe, the fight opens.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bc5 Be3 Qf6 c3 Nge7 Bc4 O-O O-O d6 Nxc6 Nxc6 Bxc5 dxc5
beats.say: 9.Nxc6 Nxc6 10.Bxc5 dxc5 — White cashes in the central tension. Trading the knights and the dark-squared bishops leaves Black with doubled c-pawns and hands White the cleaner structure plus the safer king. The dynamic Scotch has steered into a small but durable positional plus — exactly the kind of edge the open centre was meant to produce.
beats.sayShort: Nxc6, Bxc5 — trade into Black's doubled c-pawns.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bc5 Be3 Qf6 c3 Nge7 Bc4 O-O O-O d6 Nxc6 Nxc6 Bxc5 dxc5 f4
beats.say: 11.f4 — White claims the initiative on the kingside. The pawn grabs space, prepares f4-f5 to cramp Black further, and opens a future attacking front while Black is busy untangling his doubled queenside pawns. With the bishop pair gone and the better structure secured, White simply plays for the long-term squeeze.
beats.sayShort: f4 — grab kingside space, prepare f5.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bc5 Be3 Qf6 c3 Nge7 Bc4 O-O O-O d6 Nxc6 Nxc6 Bxc5 dxc5 f4 Be6 Bb5
beats.say: 11…Be6 develops the last minor piece and offers a trade of light-squared bishops; White slides to 12.Bb5, pinning and pressuring the c6-knight that holds Black's position together. The plan is clear and Capablanca-clean: trade into the structure, target the weak doubled pawns, and let the healthier majority decide the game.
beats.sayShort: Be6 Bb5 — pin and press the c6-knight.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bc5 Be3 Qf6 c3 Nge7 Bc4 O-O O-O d6 Nxc6 Nxc6 Bxc5 dxc5 f4 Be6 Bb5 Rad8
beats.say: 12…Rad8 centralises a rook and we reach the Classical Scotch middlegame: White with the sounder structure, the f4-f5 space, and pressure on the c6-knight; Black with the bishop pair gone and doubled c-pawns to nurse. That is the Scotch in one breath — strike d4 early, plant the knight, open the lines, trade into a clean edge. The other tabs show the opening's other faces: the sharp Mieses, the dashing Scotch Gambit, the solid Four Knights, and Kasparov's own Nb3 weapon.
beats.sayShort: Rad8 — the Classical edge: structure and space.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Nf6
beats.say: The Mieses is the sharpest, most modern Scotch — the line Kasparov used to put the whole opening back on the map. Black answers 4…Nf6, developing with a hit on the e4-pawn instead of pinning the knight. White must react, and the choice that follows defines the variation.
beats.sayShort: …Nf6 — the modern Mieses, hitting e4.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nxc6 bxc6 e5
beats.say: 5.Nxc6 bxc6 6.e5! The point. White trades the proud knight to damage Black's pawns — the doubled c-pawns appear — and then thrusts e5, kicking the f6-knight away and seizing a big space advantage in the centre. Black's structure is compromised; White's pawn on e5 is a thorn.
beats.sayShort: Nxc6, e5! — wreck the pawns, gain space.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nxc6 bxc6 e5 Qe7
beats.say: 6…Qe7 — Black's best. Rather than retreat the knight to a sad square, Black pins the e5-pawn to the king down the e-file, forcing White to spend a move propping it. This counterpunch is why the Mieses is so sharp: Black accepts the wrecked structure in return for active, annoying piece play.
beats.sayShort: …Qe7 — pin the e5-pawn, fight back.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nxc6 bxc6 e5 Qe7 Qe2 Nd5 c4
beats.say: 7.Qe2 defends the e5-pawn and unpins, 7…Nd5 hops the knight to a fine central square, and 8.c4! challenges it at once. White uses the space to gain tempo, kicking the knight and clamping the queenside. The plan is to keep expanding while Black's doubled c-pawns sit as a long-term target.
beats.sayShort: Qe2, c4 — defend e5, kick the d5-knight.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nxc6 bxc6 e5 Qe7 Qe2 Nd5 c4 Ba6 b3
beats.say: 8…Ba6 is the thematic pin — the bishop rakes the a6-f1 diagonal and pressures the c4-pawn, daring White to weaken. 9.b3 calmly props c4 and prepares to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop to a3, where it will hit Black's queen and dark squares. White keeps untangling without conceding the space edge.
beats.sayShort: …Ba6 b3 — pin meets a calm prop.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nxc6 bxc6 e5 Qe7 Qe2 Nd5 c4 Ba6 b3 g6 Ba3 d6
beats.say: 9…g6 prepares to fianchetto and blunt White's light squares, 10.Ba3 spears the queen on e7 down the a3-f8 diagonal, and 10…d6 strikes at the e5-spearhead to free the position. We've reached the Mieses tabiya: White enjoys more space and the healthier pawns; Black has the bishop pair and active pieces. A genuinely double-edged modern battleground — exactly why Kasparov trusted it.
beats.sayShort: Ba3 d6 — space vs the bishop pair.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Bc4
beats.say: The Scotch Gambit — pure romance. Instead of recapturing on d4, White plays 4.Bc4, leaving the pawn alive and slamming the bishop onto the f7-diagonal. The idea is speed: White develops with threats and counts on a lead in development to outweigh a single pawn. The d4-pawn can wait; the initiative cannot.
beats.sayShort: Bc4 — gambit the pawn, aim at f7.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Bc4 Nf6 e5 d5
beats.say: 4…Nf6 5.e5! White doesn't defend e4 — he pushes past it, attacking the f6-knight and grabbing space. Black hits back with 5…d5, the only good move: it forks the c4-bishop and shields the knight. The centre is a tangle of tension, and both sides must play precisely.
beats.sayShort: e5 d5 — push past, Black forks the bishop.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Bc4 Nf6 e5 d5 Bb5 Ne4 Nxd4
beats.say: 6.Bb5 sidesteps the fork and pins the c6-knight; 6…Ne4 grabs an active outpost; and 7.Nxd4 — White finally collects the gambit pawn back, the knight returning to its beloved central square. Material is level again, but White has gained time and a grip on the centre. The 'gambit' was really just a clever move-order to reach a comfortable Scotch.
beats.sayShort: Bb5, Nxd4 — pin, then regain the pawn.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Bc4 Nf6 e5 d5 Bb5 Ne4 Nxd4 Bd7 Bxc6 bxc6 O-O
beats.say: 7…Bd7 unpins and 8.Bxc6 bxc6 trades into the familiar doubled c-pawns — White's recurring Scotch dividend — before 9.O-O brings the king to safety. White has emerged from the sharp gambit skirmish with the sounder structure and a fully coordinated position, exactly the practical edge the line is built to produce.
beats.sayShort: Bxc6, O-O — doubled pawns, king safe.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Bc4 Nf6 e5 d5 Bb5 Ne4 Nxd4 Bd7 Bxc6 bxc6 O-O Bc5 Be3 Bxd4
beats.say: 9…Bc5 develops with a hit on the d4-knight, 10.Be3 defends and offers a trade, and 10…Bxd4 takes it. We've reached the Scotch Gambit tabiya: roughly level material, but White owns the better structure thanks to Black's tripled-up c-pawns and the open lines from the early skirmish. The romantic gambit has matured into a clean, pressable middlegame — the modern verdict on a 19th-century idea.
beats.sayShort: Bc5 Bxd4 — the tabiya: White presses the structure.

_key: Scotch Four Knights (4...Nf6 5.Nc3 Bb4 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.Bd3 d5)
title: Scotch Game — The Four Knights

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3
beats.say: Against 4…Nf6, White can also play the solid 5.Nc3, defending the e4-pawn and transposing into Scotch Four Knights territory. This is the choice for a player who wants a sound, classical battle rather than the sharp space-grab of the Mieses. Symmetrical development, a clear structure, a long strategic game.
beats.sayShort: Nc3 — the solid Four Knights, guarding e4.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 Bb4 Nxc6 bxc6 Bd3 d5
beats.say: 5…Bb4 pins the c3-knight, 6.Nxc6 bxc6 hands Black the doubled c-pawns again, and after 7.Bd3 Black frees himself with 7…d5, the classic central freeing break. Black accepts the slightly worse structure to get rapid development and a compact, solid centre. White will play to prove the doubled pawns matter.
beats.sayShort: Bb4, d5 — pin, then Black's freeing break.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 Bb4 Nxc6 bxc6 Bd3 d5 exd5 cxd5 O-O O-O
beats.say: 8.exd5 cxd5 9.O-O O-O — the centre clears and both sides castle. Black has rebuilt a healthy-looking centre with the d5-pawn, but the queenside pawns remain split. The position is solid and near-symmetrical; this is the quiet, manoeuvring face of the Scotch, where small structural facts decide the game over many moves.
beats.sayShort: exd5 O-O — clear the centre, both castle.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 Bb4 Nxc6 bxc6 Bd3 d5 exd5 cxd5 O-O O-O Bg5
beats.say: 10.Bg5 develops with a pin on the f6-knight, increasing the pressure on the d5-pawn and the dark squares. This is the standard plan against the isolated-from-its-brother d5-pawn: pile up on it, trade the defenders, and make the structural weakness tell. Quiet moves, deep purpose.
beats.sayShort: Bg5 — pin f6, lean on the d5-pawn.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 Bb4 Nxc6 bxc6 Bd3 d5 exd5 cxd5 O-O O-O Bg5 c6 Ne2 Bd6 Ng3 h6
beats.say: 10…c6 braces d5, 11.Ne2 reroutes the knight toward greener pastures, 11…Bd6 eyes the kingside, and 12.Ng3 lands the knight where it pressures f5 and supports a kingside build-up; 12…h6 makes luft. We've reached the Four Knights tabiya: a balanced, classical middlegame where White probes the hanging d5-pawn and the knight heads for f5. Patience and structure, the strategic heart of the Scotch.
beats.sayShort: Ne2-g3 — reroute the knight toward f5.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bc5 Nb3
beats.say: Kasparov's own favourite. Against 4…Bc5, instead of defending the knight with Be3, White simply retreats it: 5.Nb3. The point is to sidestep the pin and the trades entirely — the knight nudges the c5-bishop and White keeps a flexible, fully intact position. It's the highest-level treatment of the Classical Scotch.
beats.sayShort: Nb3 — Kasparov's retreat, dodge the pin.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bc5 Nb3 Bb6 Nc3 Nf6
beats.say: 5…Bb6 tucks the bishop onto the safe a7-g1 diagonal, and 6.Nc3 Nf6 sees both sides complete natural development around the e4-pawn. White has avoided every early trade and kept all his pieces — a small, durable edge in flexibility that a great technician can squeeze for fifty moves.
beats.sayShort: Bb6, Nc3 Nf6 — quiet, flexible development.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bc5 Nb3 Bb6 Nc3 Nf6 Qe2 d6 Be3
beats.say: 7.Qe2 connects the plan — White intends long castling — 7…d6 props the centre, and 8.Be3 offers to trade the dark-squared bishops on b6. Removing Black's good bishop suits White's setup, and the queen on e2 already looks toward the kingside and the coming pawn storm.
beats.sayShort: Qe2 Be3 — prep O-O-O, offer the bishop trade.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bc5 Nb3 Bb6 Nc3 Nf6 Qe2 d6 Be3 Bxe3 Qxe3 O-O O-O-O
beats.say: 8…Bxe3 9.Qxe3 O-O 10.O-O-O — and the battle lines are drawn. White castles queenside and the rook on d1 lines up against the d6-pawn and the half-open d-file. With the kings on opposite wings, this becomes a race: White storms the kingside with his pawns, Black the queenside. Sharp, rich, and exactly the fighting chess Kasparov wanted from a 'quiet' opening.
beats.sayShort: O-O-O — opposite castling, the race begins.

beats.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bc5 Nb3 Bb6 Nc3 Nf6 Qe2 d6 Be3 Bxe3 Qxe3 O-O O-O-O Be6 f3
beats.say: 10…Be6 develops and challenges the b3-knight's outpost on c5, and 11.f3 anchors e4 and signals the coming g4-g5 pawn storm against Black's king. We've reached the Nb3 tabiya: opposite-side castling, mutual attacks, White a half-step ahead with the more natural pawn-storm. This is why a World Champion chose the Scotch — the 'simple' opening hides the sharpest of middlegames.
beats.sayShort: Be6 f3 — anchor e4, prepare the g-pawn storm.
